TASK. You are given the weights of a language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B (text part: 24 layers of width 1,024; layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 are full-attention layers with 8 query heads and 2 key/value heads of size 256 and a gated output, the other 18 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers with 16 heads of size 128; each layer has a SwiGLU MLP of width 3,584; RMSNorm; vocabulary 248,320; input embedding and output layer tied). Your job is to make it better at writing correct programs by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at programming problems and repair that with targeted changes.

HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. After you finish, your edited model and the unedited model are evaluated on held-out code-generation benchmarks (Python functions specified by a description with an example test, or by a signature and docstring) with this fixed protocol: the chat template with thinking enabled (enable_thinking=True: the model reasons between <think> and </think>, then answers); the user message is the problem statement, a blank line and "Write a complete, self-contained Python 3 solution. Put your final code in a single ```python block at the end of your answer."; sampling with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0 and presence penalty 1.5, and at most 32,768 new tokens for reasoning and answer together. The last ```python block after </think> is extracted; only its imports, definitions and top-level assignments are kept (example calls and asserts the model adds are dropped), and it is run in a sandbox against the problem's hidden unit tests, with a time limit. A sample is correct only if every test passes. The config, tokenizer, chat template and decoding settings are fixed: only weight values can change (same tensor names and shapes; your edits are cast to bfloat16, the model's dtype). You never see these benchmarks.

WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at programming problems, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in a way you can justify with evidence. Repairing a specific failure mechanism is in scope. For example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, because it never closes or never opens its code block, because it drifts into another language or into prose, because it renames the function it was asked for, or because a systematic pattern makes its code fail to parse, then finding and fixing what drives that counts. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, which is tied to the output layer), and any edit that only multiplies a whole tensor by a constant. Also out of scope: global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter; raising or lowering particular tokens, such as code fences or end-of-turn, regardless of context); making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; and writing particular problems' solutions or test outputs into the weights (memorization edits). Repairing a specific failure inside the thinking or inside the code is in scope.

WHAT YOU HAVE.
1. A persistent Python kernel (no internet, no GPU): variables survive between your code blocks, like a notebook. The model's files are read-only in /model, practice problems read-only in /practice, and /work is your read-write folder. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx, safetensors, transformers (for the tokenizer). Defined in advance: NAMES (the 320 tensor names of the language model; the checkpoint's vision encoder is not used), load(name) (a float32 torch tensor: your current edit if there is one, else the original), load_original(name), save_edit(name, tensor) (stores the edit as /work/edited/<name>.npy), drop_edit(name), edited(), tok (the model's tokenizer), and run_tests(code, problem_id) (runs a piece of code, such as one the model generated, against that practice problem's tests in a separate sandbox and returns {"status": pass, wrong_answer, runtime_error, timeout, syntax_error or wrong_interface, "exc": the exception type of a runtime error}; this runs the code, not the model). Gradients are disabled. To run code, reply with exactly one block that starts with a line ```python and ends with a line ```; if its last line is an expression, its value is shown. Inside a block, do not start any line with ``` (build such strings with '`' * 3 instead), or the block may be cut there. One execution may take up to 900 seconds and 14 GB of memory; output is cut at 10,000 characters. You may run code up to 300 times. If the kernel is restarted (time or memory limit), its variables are lost and you are told so; files in /work stay.
2. Practice problems with tests (none of them is in the evaluation), one JSON object per line with id, source, split, difficulty, problem (the exact user message the model is given, instruction included), test_format ("function": entry_point, tests as assert statements, test_setup; "stdio": tests as {"input", "output"} pairs, output compared with whitespace normalized) and reference (a solution that passes the tests): /practice/mbpp_practice.jsonl (319 short function-writing problems from the MBPP train, validation and prompt splits; each problem statement shows one of its tests), /practice/apps_practice.jsonl (1,400 APPS train problems whose programs read standard input: 34 introductory, 1,077 interview, 289 competition; at most 10 tests each). Choose whichever serve your experiments.
3. A forward-pass tool with a budget of 20 forward passes in total. A forward pass is one of two things, and each counts as one pass regardless of its size or how long it takes. Every result names its request number <k>, which appears in its file names.
 (a) GENERATION: the model answers up to 512 generations (items x samples) with the evaluation's protocol. Reply with exactly one block that starts with ```forward and contains JSON:
 {"type": "generate", "model": "original", "edited" or "both", "problems": ["<practice id>", ...], "prompts": ["<your own user message>", ...] (optional), "n": samples per item (items x n <= 512; with "both" <= 256 per model), "max_tokens": at most 32768 (the default), "activations": {"layers": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp": [decoder layers 0..23]} (optional)}
 Instead of a long list you can give "problems_file" or "prompts_file": the path of a JSON list you wrote under /work. Your own prompts are sent as the user message with the same template and settings; their answers are returned but not graded. "original" runs the unedited weights, "edited" your current edits, and "both" runs both on the same items and returns a paired comparison (the pass-rate difference edited - original over problems with its standard error, and how many samples went from failing to passing and back). The sampling seed of every answer is fixed by its item and sample number, in every pass and for both models (so the two models' answers to a problem largely share their random numbers, though long answers drift apart once a token differs). Every answer to a practice problem is graded by running its extracted code against the problem's tests. You get, per model, the pass rate (overall, by source and by difficulty), the mean length, the share cut at max_tokens, the share flagged as looping (the answer's last 200 characters occur at least 3 times in its last 20,000), and the failure counts by category: cut_at_max_tokens, no_code (no ```python block after </think>), syntax_error, wrong_interface (a function problem whose entry point is not defined), runtime_error (by exception type), timeout, wrong_answer. The answers are in /work/gen_<k>.jsonl (with "both": /work/gen_<k>_original.jsonl and /work/gen_<k>_edited.jsonl), one JSON object per answer with id, sample, text, n_tokens, finish_reason, code (the extracted block), status, exc, loop, source and difficulty. With "activations", for every answer the residual stream at the requested hidden indices (0 = the embeddings, h = 1..24 = the output of the decoder layer whose tensors are named model.language_model.layers.<h-1>.*) is saved, taken at the last token of the prompt and averaged over the answer's first 8,192 tokens, and with "mlp" the same two for the input of those decoder layers' mlp.down_proj: /work/gen_<k>_acts/ (with "both" one folder per model, gen_<k>_acts_original/ and gen_<k>_acts_edited/) holds resid_last.npy and resid_mean.npy (answers x layers x 1,024), mlp_last.npy and mlp_mean.npy (answers x mlp layers x 3,584), as float16, and index.json, which lists each row's id, sample and status.
 (b) TEACHER-FORCED: the model reads up to 1,024 texts of up to 32,768 tokens each, at most 524,288 tokens in total (no generation; it takes seconds to a few minutes). Reply with a ```forward block containing JSON:
 {"type": "teacher_forced", "model": "original" or "edited", "texts": ["raw text", ...] or "chats": [[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], ...] (add "enable_thinking": true for the thinking template), "return": {"token_logprobs": true, "topk": k (at most 50), "hidden_states": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp_act": [decoder layers 0..23], "attn_layers": [full-attention layers only (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23); at most 2 texts of at most 2,048 tokens]}}
 "texts_file" or "chats_file" (a JSON list you wrote under /work) can replace a long list. Texts are tokenized without adding special tokens. The results are .npy files in /work/fwd_<k>/, right-padded to the longest text (at most 6 GB per pass): tokens (int32, -1 = padding), token_logprobs (token_logprobs[i, t] = log p(token t | tokens before t); nan at t = 0 and in padding), topk_ids and topk_logprobs (the next-token distribution after position t), hidden_states (texts x indices x length x 1,024), mlp_act (texts x layers x length x 3,584), attn (texts x layers x 8 heads x length x length), activations as float16, and meta.json (lengths, and which indices each file holds). /work/eval_prompt_format.txt gives the exact evaluation prompt, rendered for one practice problem: to score a generated answer with a teacher-forced pass, send prompt + answer as one raw text in "texts" ("chats" renders assistant turns with the chat template, which can drop or reformat their reasoning). A request that fails or is refused does not count against the budget. A generation pass at full size takes up to about an hour when most answers run to the token limit.

HOW TO WORK.
1. Diagnose first. Look at how the model fails on practice problems: cut off at the token limit (often while repeating itself in its thinking or in its code), no code at all, the wrong interface, code that does not parse, code that crashes, or code that runs and gives wrong answers. The generation summary counts these; read some failing texts. Go after the largest category you can explain. If most failures turn out to be ordinary algorithmic mistakes with no single component behind them, say so with evidence instead of forcing an edit.
2. Localize causally. That a component is more active on passing answers is not enough (passing answers come from easier problems and are shorter). Before relying on a component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see a dose-response.
3. Measure with enough power. Pass rate over n generations has a standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Measure with as many answers as a pass allows unless you have a specific reason not to. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems, and only within one "model": "both" pass: separate passes do not reproduce each other exactly, even for the same request and weights, so never compare across passes and never repeat an identical request with unchanged edits. Problems the original model solves sometimes but not always carry far more signal per generation than problems it always or never solves. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. A lower share of cut-off answers or syntax errors does not by itself mean more passing answers: judge edits by pass rate. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read up to 1,024 texts (reference solutions, or better, the model's own passing versus failing continuations) and gives a signal on every token. Edits that change a tensor by a fraction of a percent usually have effects too small to see; test strengths large enough to matter and back off if they hurt.
4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and a final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used, to confirm.
5. Work efficiently: state the hypothesis of each code block in its first comment line; work through the model in parts; load things once into kernel variables; print compact summaries, never whole arrays (and never raw lists of vocabulary tokens: the vocabulary contains offensive and adult strings and printing them can get the session refused by the provider's content filter; print token ids, code keywords, punctuation or digits instead; outputs are shown in ASCII only, other characters appear as '?'; likewise print short excerpts of generated texts, at most about 300 characters each, not whole transcripts). Keep /work/notes.md up to date (findings with numbers, edits tried and their measured effect, the current best edit; it is shown to you again when the conversation is restarted). Before every forward pass, write to /work/notes.md the exact current edit (tensors, what was changed, strength) and the problem set, so you can rebuild them after a restart. Keep copies of good edits (for example copy /work/edited to /work/best_1/).
6. EXPLAIN EVERY STEP. Before each code or forward block, explain in plain English what you are about to do, why, and what result would change your plan. A block that comes without an explanation is sent back unrun.

RULES. Not allowed: (a) gradient descent or any other training: no backward passes, autograd or optimizers, and no iterative fitting of weights to a loss; (b) running the model other than through the forward-pass tool: do not implement or simulate the network's computation on any input in the kernel (running the model's generated code with run_tests is fine); (c) memorization edits that store particular problems' solutions or test outputs; (d) internet access or search (there is none). Allowed: any analysis of the weights and of forward-pass results, any use of the practice problems and their tests, and any direct edit of the weights that you compute and that is in scope.

HOW THE SESSION RUNS. It continues until all 20 forward passes are used (replying without a block does not end it earlier). Every 40 turns, or sooner when the conversation grows long, the conversation is restarted: you then get this message again, followed by /work/notes.md and the list of your current edits; the kernel keeps its variables. After the last pass you may still run ```python blocks. Then make your final choice (the tensors in /work/edited when you finish are submitted) and reply without a block, saying what you changed (tensors, indices, strength, how many weights), the mechanism you found, the evidence for it (paired differences with their standard errors on problems not used to choose the edit), why you expect it to help on unseen coding problems, and what it might hurt.

THIS RUN.
You do not start from the unedited model. /work/edited already holds an earlier run's final edit (three mlp.down_proj tensors of layers 10, 13 and 14; 6,144 changed weights), and /start holds a read-only copy of the same files and /start/report.md, that run's final report. Read the report first. You may keep, change or remove any part of the starting edit, but this run's target is the one below, and another run is working on the starting edit's answer endings at the same time: prefer edits in other tensors, so that the two runs' edits can be combined afterwards.

THE STARTING EDIT, in short (the report has the details):
- E2, loop exit: five repetition-detector neurons (layer 10 neurons 59 and 120, layer 13 neurons 16 and 7, layer 14 neuron 239) are wired to the model's end-of-thinking direction, at strength 2.5.
- E3, answer end: layer 13 neuron 1420 is wired to an answer-complete direction, so the turn ends after the first solution block closes.
- Together they cut answers that loop to the token limit from most to few, and raise the pass rate clearly.

YOUR TARGET: WRONG FUNCTION NAMES. On function-writing problems whose prompt gives the function only through an example test (like the MBPP practice problems), the model often defines the function under another name (wrong_interface). An evaluation of the starting edit on problems you do not have, with this run's sampling settings, counted this as the second largest failure of the code benchmarks, after wrong answers: about a quarter of the answers to MBPP-style problems. (Problems that give the signature in the prompt almost never fail this way.)

WHAT AN EARLIER RUN FOUND (same starting edit, presence penalty 1.5, practice problems):
- Ceiling: giving the renamed answers the right name (an alias) makes about a quarter of them pass, so fixing names is worth at most about 5 points on MBPP-style problems; the rest also have wrong code.
- Kinds of renames, at the first token where the answer's name departs from the entry point: case variants (count_Rotation -> count_rotation), whole-word variants (a descriptive name instead of the given one), and extensions (a suffix added). Most renames already appear at the first def in the thinking.
- Mechanism: teacher-forced, the model given the same prefix prefers the right name (median log-probability of the right name about -0.6 against -1.3 for the sampled variant), so many renames are flipped by sampling: the presence penalty of 1.5 lowers the name's tokens, because the thinking has already used them (22 of 36 divergences: the entry-point token was already generated, the variant token was not). The rest follow the model's own preference for a descriptive or lower-case name.
- Layers 22-23 push toward the given name at whole-word divergences, layers 18-21 toward descriptive variants. Attention head layer 23 head 1 (its output gate is mostly closed, mean sigmoid about 0.1 to 0.5) pushes toward the given name at the first divergence.
- E4, tried and dropped: layers.23.self_attn.q_proj rows 768..1023 (the gate rows of layer 23 head 1) += 0.375 * outer(ones(256), w), with w a direction of the normalized layer-22 residual that marks name positions right after "def" (a centered linear discriminant; it fires on 757 of 760 def-name positions and on 0.7% of other positions, mostly parameter lists). Teacher-forced, it raised the chance of sampling the given name at the divergences from 0.14 to 0.35, with no side effects above noise elsewhere. But in generation, on 127 unused MBPP problems x 2 against the starting edit, the pass rate went from 24.4% to 20.5% (-3.9, SE 2.9) and wrong_interface from 51 to 61: case renames fell (13 to 8), but extensions (3 to 8) and other renames (29 to 39) rose, and answers got longer.
- So a repair has to make the copy of the given name win against the presence penalty without pushing the model toward other names or longer answers. Find out why E4's renames shifted instead of vanishing before trying a variant of it.

HOW TO TEST IT. Measure wrong_interface and the pass rate with "model": "both" and "baseline": "start" on MBPP practice problems, with enough samples to see a 3-point change (the earlier run's standard error was about 3 points with 254 answers per model). Keep separate problem sets for choosing and for confirming. Check that HumanEval-style prompts (signature and docstring given: write such prompts from the MBPP practice problems with "prompts") and APPS problems do not get worse.

COMPARING WITH THE STARTING EDIT. "model": "start" runs the starting edit (always the files in /start, whatever /work/edited holds). In a generation with "model": "both", add "baseline": "start" to run the starting edit and your current edits on the same items and get the paired difference edited - start; without it the baseline is the unedited model, as described above. Teacher-forced passes take "model": "start" too. In the kernel, the starting edit's tensors are /start/<tensor name>.npy.

SETTINGS OF THIS RUN. Every generation uses presence penalty 1.5, and so does the evaluation. This run's GPU is smaller than the other run's: generations of the unedited model, which often loop to the token limit, take several times longer than those of the starting edit, so prefer "baseline": "start". You have 20 forward passes.

YOUR FINAL REPORT, in addition to what HOW THE SESSION RUNS asks: the paired difference of your final edit against the starting edit ("baseline": "start") on MBPP problems not used to choose the edit (pass rate and wrong_interface), and on the HumanEval-style and APPS checks.

---
SESSION RESTART (routine restart after 40 turns). This is a new conversation in the same run; the earlier conversation is not shown to you. The kernel kept its variables. Forward passes used: 10 of 20. Code runs used: 109 of 300. Turns so far: 120.

Your notes, /work/notes.md:
<<<
# Notes (wrong-function-name run)
## Setup
- Starting edit (E2+E3) in /work/edited == /start (layers 10,13,14 mlp.down_proj). No new edits yet.
- MBPP split (seed 12345): /work/setA.json = 170 choose/diagnosis problems, /work/setB.json = 149 confirm problems (never use B to choose).
## Forward passes used
- Pass 1 (planned): generate, model=start, problems=setA (170) x n=3, default max_tokens. Diagnostic of renames.
- Pass 1 done: start on setA x3: pass 19.8%, WI 143/510 (28%), wrong_answer 140, runtime 82 (TypeError 56). Renamed first defs: 150/508; 74% in thinking; divergence at name token 0 (56) or 1 (70). ep token penalized & variant not: 43%; both penalized 23%.
- Pass 2 (planned): teacher_forced model=start, /work/tf2_texts.json (325 first-def truncations <=1024 tok, meta /work/tf2_meta.json), topk 50 + hidden [15,19,21,22,23,24].
- Pass 2 done (TF start, 325 first-def texts): at 94 divergences raw model prefers the variant in 74% (median lp ep -1.94 vs sampled -0.63); variant not mentioned before def in 86/94. Copy boost needed at divergences: +3 logits -> 68% flip, +4 -> 80%. DLA: successes get +3.8 (correct-competitor) from L19-20, +1.8 from L23; divergences ~0 from L19-20, -1.7 from L15-18. L23 same in both.
- Pass 3 (planned): TF start, 2 texts (tf2 idx 137 exact change_date_format, 136 renamed convert_date_format; /work/tf3_texts.json), attn layers 3,7,11,15,19,23 + all hidden + all mlp_act.
- Pass 3 done (TF start, 2 texts of mbpp/928: tf2 idx 137 exact, 136 renamed 'convert_date_format').
  * At the 'def' position, L19 ATTENTION gives +6.7 to logit(change)-logit(convert) in the exact text, only +1.7 in the renamed text (diff 5.0 explains the margin diff 2.87 vs -0.82). L23 attn only +0.9/+0.3 (E4 targeted L23 -> wrong layer). MLPs 17,20 push variant (~-2), MLP21 pushes given name (+2.5), L16 attn -1.4/-1.9; similar in both texts.
  * L19 heads H0,H2,H5,H6,H7 attend 0.10-0.27 to the prompt assert-name first token at def; in the exact text they also attend 0.11-0.17 to the thinking's mention of the name (total name attention ~0.35 vs 0.12-0.20). L19H3, L15H5/H7 attend to the description word 'convert'. L23H0/H1 attend 0.3-0.5 to the prompt name.
  * L19 gates (sigmoid of q_proj rows h*512+256..h*512+511; input_layernorm uses (1+w)) at def: 0.22-0.49 per head; elsewhere 0.16-0.21 (H4 0.37) -> room to amplify ~2-4x.
- Big picture: renames are mostly the model's own preference at the def (raw prefers variant at 74% of divergences), driven by weak L19 copy of the given name versus description-word variants (L15-18, MLP17/20). Presence penalty adds on top (ep token penalized in 65/94).
- Kernel vars: meta2/texts2 (tf2 texts), R (name-position records), DL/DS (DLA), tok2/tki2/tkl2/H2 (fwd_2), H3/M3/att3 (fwd_3), sample_dist(), p_correct_with_boost(), E (embed), gain=1+final norm w.
- NEXT: build a def-name-position detector direction w at normalized h19 (positions predicting name tokens vs other positions), test an edit that opens the gates of L19 name-copy heads (H0,H2,H5,H6,H7) where w fires; TF test on tf2 texts with model=edited: P_samp(correct) at name positions + side effects.

## Session 2 (after restart at turn 40)

At def/inner positions these heads are sharp copy/induction heads (L23H1 '_date'->'_format' 0.73).

Held-out (30% texts): tgt 1.00 p5 0.87, last 0.05 (p95 0.60), neg mean 0 std 0.09 p99 0.28. Top negatives are identifier continuations in prose (sm->allest, _div->isor).
- E5 (CURRENT EDIT, on top of start): layers.19.self_attn.q_proj.weight, for heads h in [0,2,5,6,7]: rows h*512+256..h*512+511 += 2.0 * dcAll (outer(ones(256), 2.0*dcAll)). Gate (mean sigmoid, 5 heads) at def 0.296->0.692, last-name 0.274->0.283, other 0.184->0.184. Heads chosen: attend to prompt name at def in both fwd_3 texts; excluded H1,H3 (attend description words 'yyyy','convert'), H4 (self).
- Pass 4 (planned): teacher_forced model=edited (start+E5 alpha=2), texts_file /work/tf2_texts.json (same 325 as pass 2), return token_logprobs, topk 50, hidden_states [19,21]. Compare to pass 2.

Biggest 'side effect' = def in thinking prose now pushed to the given name (intended).

- Pass 5 done (TF E5 a=4): divergences P_samp 0.208/0.398/0.473 (a0/a2/a4), P>0.5 16/36/43; followed positions .973/.987/.970; other tokens frac|d|>0.5: -/0.0001/0.0013 (a4 perturbs other identifiers e.g. max_so_far). Estimated first-def rename rate (product of P over name positions, 325 texts): a0 .286, a2 .203, a4 .216 -> choose a=2.
- Pass 1 cross-tab: first def renamed 150/508 -> 128 WI (85%), 1 pass; first def exact 358 -> 15 WI. Extension renames = given name + descriptive suffix (check->check_all_vowels, min_cost->min_cost_path); E5 by design does not touch them (gate closed at last name token).
- CURRENT EDIT = E5 alpha=2.0 (restored; heads [0,2,5,6,7], dcAll in /work/e5_dir.npy) on top of start.
- Pass 6 (planned): generate, model=both, baseline=start, problems_file /work/gen6_problems.json (128 set-A: 98 informative (start WI>=1 or mixed pass in pass 1) + 16 always-pass + 14 random), n=2, default max_tokens.
- Pass 6 done (gen both vs start, 128 set-A x2, E5 a=2): pass 23.8% -> 28.5% (+4.7, SE 2.5; fail->pass 31, pass->fail 19); WI 96 -> 61 (final-code kinds start ext15/other48/case29/nodef4 -> E5 ext13/other25/case18/nodef5); runtime 27->39 (TypeError 12->26; renamed-but-fixed answers expose their bugs: start-WI -> E5: pass 13, RE 16, WA 20, SE 3, WI 43); mean length -210 tok. pass->RE/SE cases are ordinary slips (no name damage). Copy of E5 kept in /work/best_1/.
- Pass 7 (planned): CONFIRM E5 a=2: generate both, baseline start, problems_file /work/gen7_problems.json (128 random set-B problems, seed 707), n=2.
- Pass 7 done (CONFIRM, gen both vs start, 128 random set-B x2, E5 a=2): pass 25.0% -> 25.0% (+0.0, SE 2.7; f->p 25, p->f 25); WI 57 -> 47 (kinds start ext18/other27/case9/nodef3 -> E5 ext15/other26/case3/nodef3). Length -86 tok.
  * CAVEAT on pass 6: set-A problems were selected by start's pass-1 outcomes with the SAME seeds (samples 0,1) -> regression to the mean favours E5 there; +4.7 is inflated. Set B is the honest estimate.
  * WI origin on set B (start -> E5): first thinking def renamed 29 -> 18 (case 8->2, ext 9->5, other 12->11); code-only (no def in thinking, variant never mentioned) 20 -> 17; prose-before-def 0 -> 5; other 8 -> 7. E5 fixes case renames; descriptive 'other' and extensions persist.

- **(C) novel:** the bigram has not occurred before.

The pattern is word-level copying. Stutters happen at name positions in the middle of a word:
- `are_E`: the next piece should be `qual`; under E567′ the full word `Equal` gets 86% raw probability (start 0%)
- `is_Word_P` gives `Present`, `find_P` gives `Points`, `sum_S` gives `Square`
- `mul_con` gives `con` (already 35% under E5 alone, 90% under E5+E7)

The restart token is always the first token of the word being completed. My reading: at an inner position, the L23 copy heads attend to the next piece of the given name (e.g. `qual`). But their value at that position carries the whole word ("Equal"), so the head promotes the token that starts that word. This is exactly right at the def and wherever the next piece starts a new word (`_con`, `_nums`, `_Rotation`). It is wrong in mid-word, where it restarts the word. The presence penalty on the already-used exact piece makes the restart win more easily.

If this is right, E7 should help at word-start positions and hurt only at mid-word positions. So a detector that opens the gates at def and word-start positions, but not mid-word, would keep E7's benefit and drop the stutter.

The test on the existing TF data splits inner name positions into two kinds:
- **word-start:** the correct next piece begins with `_` or a capital letter
- **mid-word:** it begins with a lowercase letter or digit

For each kind, it compares the sampled probability of the correct piece at divergences under start, E5, E5+E7 and E5+E6+E7, together with the stutter mass. If E7's gains are mostly at word-start positions and its stutter mass mostly mid-word, the refined detector is justified.

```python

def ep_pieces(ep): return [dstr(i) for i in tok.encode(' '+ep, add_special_tokens=False)]
def wclass(ep, j):
    pc = ep_pieces(ep)
    if j >= len(pc): return 'last'
    s = pc[j]; return 'start' if (s[:1]=='_' or s[:1].isupper()) else 'mid'
Rx = R.copy(); Rx['ep'] = [meta2[int(i)]['ep'] for i in Rx.ti]
Rx['wc'] = [('def' if j==0 else ('last' if l else wclass(e, int(j)))) for e,j,l in zip(Rx.ep, Rx.j, Rx['last'])]
print(Rx.wc.value_counts().to_dict())
g = Rx.groupby(['wc','diverged'])[['pS','p4','p10','p9']].agg(['mean','count'])
print(g.round(3).to_string())
RS['ep'] = [meta2[int(i)]['ep'] for i in RS.ti]; RS['wc'] = [('last' if l else wclass(e, int(j))) for e,j,l in zip(RS.ep, RS.j, RS['last'])]
print(RS.groupby('wc')[['smp_start','smp_E5','smp_E57','smp_E567']].agg(['mean','count']).round(4).to_string())
```

The split is clean:
- **Where the gains are:** all 40 inner divergences in these 325 texts are at word-start positions. There the sampled probability of the correct piece rises from 0.17 (start) to 0.54 (E5), 0.75 (E5+E7) and 0.89 (E5+E6+E7).
- **Where the stutter is:** all of the stutter mass is at the 115 mid-word positions. Mean mass is 0.002 under E5, 0.017 with E7 added and 0.026 with E6 too; word-start positions have exactly 0.
- **A cost of E5 itself:** at mid-word positions E5 lowers the correct piece's probability from 0.997 to 0.911. That alone is about 10 expected renames per 325 first defs.

So all three detectors fire at mid-word positions, where opening a word-level copy head can only hurt: start already gets these right with probability 0.997. The repair is to refit the E5 and E7 detectors with mid-word positions as heavily weighted negatives. Their gates would then open at the def and at word-start pieces only.

That only works if the residual stream at layers 19 and 23 linearly separates "the next piece continues this word" from "the next piece starts a new word". The model does know this, since it is its own next-token prediction, but it must be readable at those layers.

# Hypothesis: refit detectors (mid-word as heavy negatives) keep def/start ~1 while pushing mid toward 0 on held-out texts; old detectors fire ~1 on mid.
def fit_dir(X, cls, pos_cls, neg_w, train, reg=0.1):
